# Bastioned fortification (trace italienne) (`bastion_fortification`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs cannon_artillery; helped by geometry_proof, surveying_triangulation, perspective_technical_drawing, field_fortification
- Core idea: High thin medieval walls are easy targets for cannon. The answer is a low, very thick rampart of rammed earth faced with brick or stone, sunk behind a wide ditch so that only its top shows above a long gentle outer slope (glacis). At every corner an arrow-shaped bastion projects, with guns in its flanks that fire along the ditch and along the faces of the neighbouring bastions. The plan is drawn so that no foot of wall is unseen by a flanking gun: there is no dead ground. An attacker can no longer storm a breach quickly and must dig his way forward for weeks.
- Pitfalls:
  - Round towers leave dead ground at their foot where miners can work unseen; the bastion's straight faces remove it
  - Building high to look strong; height is what cannon destroy
  - Earth absorbs shot, masonry shatters; an earth rampart thrown up in weeks is better than a stone wall
  - The system costs fortunes and needs a large garrison and many guns; several Italian states ruined themselves on it (Siena, 1550s)
  - A fortress only delays; without a relief army it falls in the end
- History: europe: c. 1450 – Alberti recommends angled, saw-toothed walls; 1480s – Francesco di Giorgio's and Giuliano da Sangallo's experiments (Poggio Imperiale begun 1488), so in 1490 the idea exists but almost every town still has medieval walls; 1501–1503 – Nettuno; 1515 – Civitavecchia; 1530s – Sanmicheli at Verona; 1530s–1560s – Vienna refortified with bastions after the siege of 1529; 1667–1707 – Vauban; islamic: 16th–17th c. – Ottomans besiege bastioned fortresses (Malta 1565, Candia 1648–1669, Vienna 1683) but build few themselves; india: 16th c. – Portuguese bastioned forts at Diu and Goa; china: ancient to Ming – rammed-earth city walls 10 to 20 m thick were already largely cannon-proof, which may explain the slower development of siege guns there (Andrade); east_asia: 1864 – the magistrate's office moves into Goryokaku, the star fort at Hakodate, Japan; americas: 1672–1695 – Castillo de San Marcos, Florida
- Read:
  - Christopher Duffy, Siege Warfare: The Fortress in the Early Modern World 1494–1660 (1979)
  - Geoffrey Parker, The Military Revolution (1988)
  - J. R. Hale, The Early Development of the Bastion: An Italian Chronology c. 1450–c. 1534, in Europe in the Late Middle Ages (1965)
